extracted.intended_audience: funding agencies, grant applicants, and review committees (research funders and reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for research assessment practices aimed at funding agencies and review committees to evaluate researchers and proposals fairly, emphasizing research content over journal-based metrics. Based on the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA) as adopted/implemented by HFSP.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Recommendation — do not use journal-based metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use journal-based metrics, such as Journal Impact Factors, as a surrogate measure of the quality of individual research articles, to assess an individual scientist’s contributions, or in hiring, promotion, or funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the overarching DORA principle: assessment should put the science into evaluation rather than relying on the journal in which work appears. Avoid using Impact Factor or similar journal-level metrics to judge individual papers or researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the criteria used in evaluating the scientific productivity of grant applicants and clearly highlight, especially for early-stage investigators, that the scientific content of a paper is much more important than publication metrics or the identity of the journal in which it was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding agencies and review committees should state clearly what criteria they use to judge applicants (e.g., scientific content, originality, rigor) and ensure these statements make clear that journal name/metrics are not proxies for quality. Special attention should be given to early-stage investigators in communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all research outputs, not just publications
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of research assessment, consider the value and impact of all research outputs (including datasets and software) in addition to research publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment frameworks should explicitly recognize and weigh non-traditional outputs (data, code, protocols, preprints) alongside articles. Review processes and application materials should allow and encourage applicants to describe these outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a broad range of impact measures including qualitative indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider a broad range of impact measures including qualitative indicators of research impact, such as influence on policy and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on quantitative bibliometrics; include narrative and qualitative evidence of impact (e.g., policy influence, changes to clinical practice, technological uptake). Reviewers should be instructed to value and interpret such qualitative indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize research quality over journal impact in proposal evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating research proposals HFSP places a strong emphasis on the quality of the applicants’ research and not on impact factor or journal in which the article was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, reviewers should focus their evaluation on the scientific merit, rigor, innovation, and feasibility of the proposed work and the applicant's demonstrated contributions, rather than the venue metrics of prior publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement DORA-aligned statements in application and review materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The suggested practices pertaining to HFSP are already in place in our application guidelines to applicants and review committee instructions. Therefore accepting the DORA standard does not add new procedures to our existing work flow and HFSP will add explicit statements in all application guidelines for the grant, fellowship, and CDA competitions as of 2015.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should update application instructions and reviewer guidance to explicitly state adherence to DORA principles (e.g., explicit lines telling reviewers not to use journal impact factors), and ensure these statements appear in all relevant program documentation.
